{{Short description|Test to determine whether a curve is a graph of a function}}
[[File:Graphs of the vertical line test.svg|frame|The vertical line test, shown graphically. The [[abscissa]] shows the [[domain of a function|domain of the (to be tested) function]].]]
In mathematics, the '''vertical line test''' is a visual way to determine if a [[Curve (mathematics)|curve]] is a [[graph of a function]] or not. A [[Function (mathematics)|function]] can only have one output, ''y'', for each unique input, ''x''. If a vertical line intersects a curve on an ''xy''-plane more than once then for one value of ''x'' the curve has more than one value of ''y'', and so, the curve does not represent a function. If all vertical lines intersect a curve at most once then the curve represents a function.<ref>
{{cite book | last = Stewart | first = James | title = Calculus: Concepts and Contexts | url = https://archive.org/details/studentsolutions00cole | url-access = registration |edition=2nd |page=[https://archive.org/details/studentsolutions00cole/page/17 17] | publisher = Brooks/Cole | location = Pacific Grove | year = 2001 | isbn = 978-0-534-37718-2 |quote=The Vertical Line Test: A curve in the ''xy''-plane is the graph of a function of ''x'' if and only if no vertical line intersects the curve more than once.}}
</ref>

By failing the vertical line test, a curve that does not represent a function may be described more broadly as a [[multivalued function]], where its multiple values are each the intersections with the vertical line. An example is the equation <math>y^2 = x</math>, which gives <math>y = \pm\sqrt{x}</math> when solved for <math>y</math>. Here, the <math>\pm</math> symbol yields two distinct output values, failing the vertical line test on the domain right of the Y-axis.
